doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

chapter: Opinions on jazz and big bands
title: Modern jazz and Ornette Coleman at Monterey
summary: He doesn't understand much present or free jazz and recalls first hearing Coleman.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Well it’s been a great year to live through for you, and I’ve said a number of times I always felt like I was born in the wrong era.
Well you certainly don’t have what we had.

I just can’t stomach most of the stuff I hear today. And I don’t understand it. And I always hearken back to Louis Armstrong, the boppers and this — what the hell song is it he does — “The Whiffinpoof Song.” He’s got a line in “The Whiffinpoof Song” about the boppers with the hey-de-hey and stuff. But I still don’t understand a lot of the people who are important in jazz some years back — Ornette Coleman. I mean God I’ll never forget I was at the jazz festival in Northern California, what the hell —
I think I know what you mean. Monterey.

Monterey. Thank you. The Monterey Jazz Party, and I went out to go to the bathroom and when I came back in there was this terrible noise. Woody Herman’s band was there, and the Ellington band was there, and a lot of great guys. And there was this terrible sound and this guy up there with a white plastic saxophone. And I thought for God’s sakes, what’s going on here? And that was Ornette Coleman. First time I’d heard him. And it just didn’t make any sense to me. Still doesn’t. But people like me are dying off. There aren’t many of us left you know.
Well he was innovating but what he was innovating was—
It wasn’t musically pleasing to me at all.
And he doesn’t swing by the way.
